audits.mathematicalReason: Steph's overall scoring rate is (15+10)/(20+10)=5/6, so Candace also scored 25 baskets in 30 attempts. Let her first- and second-half basket counts be x and y. The strict percentage comparisons give x/12<15/20 and y/18<1, hence x≤8 and y≤17 because the counts are integers. Together with x+y=25, these force x=8 and y=17. Therefore y−x=9. Calculating percentage rates and applying simultaneous inequalities with integer restrictions both directly match the proposed scopes.

figureEvidence.fact: The table shows Steph's half-by-half results as 15/20 and 10/10, and Candace's attempt totals as 12 and 18, with her basket counts left blank.

audits.mathematicalReason: There are 3^4=81 equally likely allowed hop histories. Returning histories split according to whether hop 2 reaches the starting leaf. If it does, there are 3·3=9 histories. Otherwise, the first two hops have 3·2 choices, and hop 3 has two nonstarting destinations that permit the final return, giving 3·2·2=12 histories. Thus the probability is 21/81=7/27. Alternatively, with p_n the return probability after n hops, p_0=1 and p_(n+1)=(1−p_n)/3, producing 0, 1/3, 2/9, and 7/27. Both optional routes are valid; neither is required in addition to the other.

figureEvidence.fact: Four leaves are shown, with the cricket initially on the left leaf. No distance or adjacency restriction is inferred from their placement; the permitted hops are specified by the text.

audits.mathematicalReason: Represent the toothpicks as grid edges forming one connected cycle, with degree 2 at every used vertex. Encode the enclosed cells by indicators t_j,m_j,b_j for the three rows, with m_0=m_9=0. Exactly one boundary edge around middle cell j means t_j+b_j=1+2m_j−m_(j−1)−m_(j+1). If every m_j is zero, connectivity forces either the entire top row or the entire bottom row to be enclosed, giving 2 loops. Otherwise the enclosed middle cells form one consecutive block: an isolated enclosed middle cell is impossible, separate blocks would be disconnected, and two omitted columns at either end would force another disconnected component. Consequently the block is [1,8], [1,7], [2,8], or [2,7]. At each block endpoint both outer-row cells are enclosed; at every internal column exactly one of the top and bottom cells is enclosed. The respective counts are 2^6, 2^5, 2^5, and 2^4. Each resulting region has one simple boundary, and taking that boundary inverts the encoding. The total is 2+64+32+32+16=146. The graph, combined-counting, and optional bijection scopes are all defensible.

figureEvidence.fact: The grid has 8 columns and 3 rows. Every cell in the middle row is labeled 1, while all cells in the top and bottom rows are unlabeled.

audits.mathematicalReason: Coincident full diagonals have the same midpoint, so all cards share a center. Let α be the acute angle between a diagonal and a long side. Then tan α=1/(2+√3)=2−√3=tan 15°, obtainable from the tangent difference formula. Thus α=15°, and each successive clockwise alignment rotates the card by 2α=30°. Set the original direction of B from the center to 0°. The four original corner directions are 0°, −30°, 150°, and 180°. Under repeated clockwise 30° rotations, their first positive arrival times at B are respectively 12, 11, 5, and 6 steps. The earliest arrival therefore occurs after five additions, using six cards total. Rectangle and trigonometric properties support this valid rotation method; they are not asserted to be the only possible method.

figureEvidence.fact: In the original upright rectangle, B is the upper-left vertex, A the upper-right vertex, and C the lower-left vertex. The second card shares the full diagonal AC and is turned clockwise relative to the first, fixing the rotation branch used.

audits.mathematicalReason: There are four possible 2×2 blocks. In any specified block, a shaded diamond requires all four triangular shaded halves to point inward, fixing all four tile orientations. Its probability is therefore (1/4)^4. Every block includes the central cell of the 3×3 grid, and the four diamond positions require four different orientations of that tile. Hence the events are mutually exclusive, and the desired probability is 4·(1/4)^4=1/64. Alternatively, any central-tile orientation selects exactly one possible diamond position; its three other tiles must match, while the remaining five tiles are unrestricted. This gives 4·4^5 favorable tilings out of 4^9. Both proposed routes correctly handle the overlap between possible positions.

figureEvidence.fact: The board is a 3×3 grid, and the four available tiles are the four orientations of a square with one diagonal half shaded.
The example contains a shaded diamond in the lower-right 2×2 block, formed by four shaded triangles whose right-angle corners meet at that block's central grid vertex.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let 0<a<b be the triangle's legs. Congruence of the four corner triangles gives a+b=√3. Their total area is 3−2=1, so each has area 1/4 and ab=1/2. Therefore (b−a)^2=(a+b)^2−4ab=1, and positivity gives b−a=1. Thus a=(√3−1)/2, b=(√3+1)/2, and a/b=2−√3. Alternatively, the hypotenuse is an inner-square side, so a²+b²=2. Setting t=a/b and combining this with (a+b)²=3 yields t²−4t+1=0; the restriction 0<t<1 selects 2−√3. The ratio node describes the target quotient, while the substantive alternative geometric and algebraic calculations are correctly represented by the supplied routes.

figureEvidence.fact: The inner square has one vertex on each outer-square side. The shaded upper-left corner triangle has legs on adjacent outer-square sides and a hypotenuse that is a side of the inner square; congruent corner triangles make each outer side the sum of a short and a long leg.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let O be the common center. Rotation gives OA=OE and ∠AOE=20°, so triangle AOE has base angle ∠EAO=80°. A square's diagonal makes ∠OAB=45°. In the displayed clockwise configuration, AB lies between AE and AO, so ∠EAB=80°−45°=35°. Alternatively, all vertices lie on the same circumcircle and the minor central angle ∠EOB is 90°−20°=70°. The corresponding inscribed angle EAB is 35°. Both proposed routes are valid and respect the diagram's angle branch.

figureEvidence.fact: A and B are the upper-left and upper-right vertices of the original square, and E is the clockwise image of A, above AB and to the right of A. This places ray AB between rays AE and AO and identifies the minor arc EB not containing A.

audits.mathematicalReason: Parallel cuts produce top triangles similar to the whole triangle. If its total area is S, the left shaded area is S[1−(11/h)^2], whereas the right shaded area is S[(h−5)/h]^2. Equating them gives h²−121=(h−5)², hence 10h=146 and h=14.6. This satisfies the necessary geometric domain h>11 and h>5. The complementary-area route is also valid: with full base b, the left unshaded triangle has area 121b/(2h), while the right unshaded trapezoid has area 5b(2h−5)/(2h). Equality yields the same equation. Similarity properties and both proposed routes match their definitions; the isosceles condition need not be separately used.

figureEvidence.fact: The left diagram shades the lower trapezoid and labels the unshaded top triangle's height 11. The right diagram shades the top triangle and labels the unshaded lower trapezoid's height 5. Both cuts are parallel to AC, and h is the full triangle height.
